nameStory: The Fork-tailed Bush Katydid gets its name from the distinctive forked shape at the tip of its abdomen, which looks like a tiny pitchfork when viewed from above. This forked tail helps distinguish it from other bush katydids that have curved or straight tail appendages. The 'bush' part of the name refers to their preference for shrubby vegetation rather than tall trees or grasslands.
description: Fork-tailed Bush Katydids are slender, green insects that look like leafy grasshoppers with extra-long antennae. They belong to the katydid family, which includes the insects famous for their 'katy-did, katy-didn't' nighttime choruses. These delicate-looking creatures have long, narrow wings that extend well beyond their bodies and thread-like antennae that can be twice as long as their entire body. Adults typically measure about 1-2 inches in length, not counting their impressive antennae.

idTips.label: Forked tail
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive Y-shaped fork at the tip of the abdomen - it feels firm and pointed if you gently touch it, unlike the smooth curves of other katydids

idTips.label: Extra-long antennae
idTips.description: Thread-thin antennae that stretch far beyond the body length, constantly moving and feeling around like delicate whips

idTips.label: Narrow green wings
idTips.description: Wings are longer than the body with visible veining that looks like leaf structure - they feel papery and rustle softly when touched

idTips.label: Slender build
idTips.description: Much more delicate and narrow-bodied than grasshoppers, with a stick-like appearance that sways gently in the breeze

idTips.label: Bush-dwelling behavior
idTips.description: Found clinging to shrubs and low vegetation rather than on the ground, moving with slow, deliberate steps

habitat: Fork-tailed Bush Katydids thrive in shrubby areas, forest edges, and gardens throughout New England's lower elevations. Look for them in dense vegetation like elderberry bushes, wild roses, and overgrown field borders where they can easily blend in with the foliage. They're particularly fond of areas where woods meet open spaces, such as hiking trail edges and suburban yards with established shrub plantings.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active, though tiny nymphs may begin hatching from overwintered eggs in late spring on warm days.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible and vocal, often found on shrubs during the day and heard calling at night with soft chirping sounds.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with mating and egg-laying occurring before the first hard frost ends their season.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity - eggs overwinter in plant stems and bark crevices, waiting for spring warmth to hatch.

funFact: Young Fork-tailed Bush Katydids can actually be agricultural pests that damage citrus fruits, but the adults become beneficial garden helpers by eating aphids and other soft-bodied insects that harm plants.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other bush katydids, but the forked tail is your best clue - if you see a 'Y' shape at the rear end, you've found your fork-tailed friend. Remember: 'Fork in the road, fork on the katydid' - other bush katydids have curved or straight tail appendages instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'bush' katydids, these insects are actually more closely related to crickets than to grasshoppers, which explains their long antennae and nighttime singing habits rather than the daytime buzzing of true grasshoppers.
compareHints: Among its bush katydid relatives in New England, the Fork-tailed is distinguished by that telltale forked rear appendage - Northern Bush Katydids have curved tails, while Broad-winged Bush Katydids have notably wider wings and straight tail projections. The fork shape is unique to this species and makes identification straightforward once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Scudderia bush katydids in New England, the northern species tends to be more common in cooler, northern areas compared to its relatives.
Among New England's bush katydids, the treetop bush katydid is distinguished by its prominent dark wing stripes and preference for high canopy living.
